subject: History
description: Covers Enfield rifle, Nana Saheb, and GOI Act 1858.

questions.stem: The spark that ignited the Revolt of 1857 was the introduction of the new Enfield rifle. What was the specific rumor regarding the cartridges of this rifle that enraged the sepoys?

options.option_text: The cartridges were greased with the fat of cows and pigs
The cartridges were intentionally manufactured with rusted iron to cause injuries
The gunpowder was mixed with crushed bones of sacred animals
The cartridges were inscribed with offensive religious symbols

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The new Enfield P-53 rifle required soldiers to bite off the end of a greased paper cartridge before loading it. A widespread rumor circulated among the sepoys that this grease was made from a mixture of beef fat (offensive to Hindus, who revere the cow) and pork fat (forbidden for Muslims). This convinced the sepoys that the British were intentionally trying to destroy their religions.
DECOY BUSTING: The "crushed bones in flour" was another rumor circulating at the time, but the specific trigger for the mutiny was the greased cartridge.
EXAM INSIGHT: Mangal Pandey of the 34th Native Infantry at Barrackpore was the first to openly mutiny against his officers over this issue on March 29, 1857, leading to his hanging.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: During the Revolt of 1857, who led the incredibly fierce and prolonged resistance against the British forces in the city of Kanpur?

options.option_text: Nana Saheb
Begum Hazrat Mahal
Kunwar Singh
Rani Lakshmibai

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Nana Saheb, the adopted son of the exiled Maratha Peshwa Baji Rao II, led the rebellion in Kanpur. The British had refused to grant him his father's pension under Dalhousie's Doctrine of Lapse. He was assisted by his brilliant military commander, Tantia Tope.
DECOY BUSTING: Begum Hazrat Mahal led the revolt in Lucknow (Awadh). Kunwar Singh, an 80-year-old Zamindar, famously led the revolt in Bihar (Arrah). Rani Lakshmibai led the revolt in Jhansi.
EXAM INSIGHT: After the recapture of Kanpur by the British under Sir Colin Campbell, Nana Saheb escaped to Nepal and was never captured or heard from again.

questions.stem: The Revolt of 1857 fundamentally changed the administration of India. Which historic document officially transferred the power to govern India from the East India Company directly to the British Crown?

options.option_text: The Government of India Act, 1858
The Indian Councils Act, 1861
The Charter Act of 1853
The Pitt's India Act, 1784

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Following the shock of the mutiny, the British Parliament passed the Government of India Act 1858 (often called the 'Act for the Good Government of India'). It abolished the East India Company entirely. The powers of government, territories, and revenues were transferred directly to the British Crown. 
DECOY BUSTING: The Pitt's India Act (1784) had previously established the dual control of the Company and the Crown. The Charter Act of 1853 introduced open competition for civil services. The Indian Councils Act 1861 started the portfolio system.
EXAM INSIGHT: Queen Victoria's Proclamation (read out by Lord Canning at the Allahabad Durbar in Nov 1858) officially announced this change. It also promised non-intervention in religious matters and the end of annexations (killing the Doctrine of Lapse).

questions.stem: Mangal Pandey, whose attack on a British officer at Barrackpore in March 1857 is widely seen as a prelude to the full revolt, belonged to which regiment of the Bengal Army?

options.option_text: 19th Native Infantry, Bengal Army
34th Native Infantry, Bengal Army
45th Native Infantry, Bengal Army
26th Native Infantry, Bengal Army

questions.explanation: Mangal Pandey was a sepoy of the 34th Bengal Native Infantry stationed at Barrackpore. He attacked Sergeant-Major Hewson on 29 March 1857 and was hanged on 8 April 1857. The 19th NI is often confused with him because that regiment was also disbanded early in 1857 over cartridge protests, but Pandey himself belonged to the 34th.

questions.stem: After the collapse of the Revolt of 1857, the last Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar was tried by a British military commission and exiled. Where did he spend his remaining years and die in November 1862?

options.option_text: Port Blair, Andaman Islands colonial prison
Rangoon (Yangon) in present-day Myanmar
Aden in Yemen, under British colonial custody
Colombo, Ceylon, under a house arrest order

questions.explanation: Bahadur Shah Zafar was tried, convicted of rebellion and treason, and exiled to Rangoon (Burma) in October 1858, where he died on 7 November 1862. Port Blair (Andaman) is a common distractor because it was used for later freedom fighters, but Zafar was never sent there — he died in British Burma.

questions.stem: Unlike Jhansi, Satara, and Nagpur — which were annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse — Awadh was annexed by Dalhousie in 1856 on a fundamentally different legal ground. What was that stated justification?

options.option_text: Absence of a legitimate male heir to the throne
Alleged misgovernance and chronic maladministration
Treaty violation by the Nawab with a rival power
Non-payment of dues under the Subsidiary Alliance

questions.explanation: Awadh's Nawab Wajid Ali Shah had a natural heir, so the Doctrine of Lapse (which required no male heir) could not apply. Dalhousie instead used the 'misgovernance' argument, invoking a clause in the 1801 treaty. This distinction is a frequent exam trap: candidates confuse the Doctrine of Lapse with the misgovernance pretext because both were Dalhousie-era annexations.

questions.stem: Nana Sahib, the leader of the revolt at Kanpur who was denied his adoptive father's pension by the East India Company, was born with what given name?

options.option_text: Tatya Tope, his most trusted field commander
Dhondu Pant, the name given to him at birth
Azimullah Khan, his principal political advisor
Nana Rao, after his adoptive Peshwa lineage

questions.explanation: Nana Sahib's real name was Dhondu Pant; 'Nana Sahib' was a title. He was the adopted son of the last Peshwa, Baji Rao II. Tatya Tope (Ramchandra Pandurang) was his general, not his birth name — a very common mix-up. Azimullah Khan was his London-based envoy who lobbied (unsuccessfully) for his pension.

questions.stem: Begum Hazrat Mahal took charge of the revolt in Lucknow and proclaimed her young son Birjis Qadr as the Nawab of Awadh. She was the wife of which ruler who had been deposed and exiled to Calcutta by the British just a year before the revolt?

options.option_text: Nawab Siraj-ud-Daula, last effective Nawab of Bengal
Nawab Wajid Ali Shah, last Nawab of Awadh
Nawab Shuja-ud-Daula, who signed the 1765 Allahabad Treaty
Nawab Asaf-ud-Daula, who built the Bara Imambara

questions.explanation: Hazrat Mahal was a consort of Nawab Wajid Ali Shah, who was deposed in 1856 and sent to Calcutta (he never returned). She led the Awadh resistance with great tenacity. Shuja-ud-Daula is a frequent distractor because he is prominently associated with the Battle of Buxar (1764), but he predates the 1857 era by nearly a century.

questions.stem: An elderly zamindar from Bihar — reportedly around 80 years old — conducted guerrilla operations against the British through 1857–58. After taking a bullet wound in his arm during a river crossing, he legendarily severed the limb himself. A postage stamp was issued in his honour. Who was this leader?

options.option_text: Raja Ram Baksh Singh, feudal lord in Uttar Pradesh
Amar Singh, who carried on the campaign after him
Kunwar Singh, zamindar of Jagdishpur in Bihar
Devi Singh, a commander active around Muzaffarpur

questions.explanation: Kunwar Singh of Jagdishpur (Bhojpur, Bihar) was approximately 80 years old during the revolt and proved a remarkable guerrilla tactician. While crossing the Ganges on 22 April 1858, he was wounded; he reportedly cut off his own forearm and offered it to the Ganga, dying days later on 26 April 1858. Amar Singh (his brother) is often confused with him because Amar Singh continued the Bihar campaign after Kunwar's death, but the famous arm incident belongs to Kunwar Singh alone.

questions.stem: Which nationalist author first systematically reframed the events of 1857 as 'The Indian War of Independence' — challenging the British dismissal of the uprising as a mere 'Sepoy Mutiny' — in a book completed while he was in London in 1909?

options.option_text: Bal Gangadhar Tilak, writing in his Marathi newspaper Kesari
Vinayak Damodar Savarkar, in his 1909 historical monograph
Surendranath Banerjee, in his memoir 'A Nation in Making'
Bipin Chandra Pal, in his nationalist writings on Indian identity

questions.explanation: V. D. Savarkar wrote 'The Indian War of Independence, 1857' while studying law in London. The British authorities banned it before publication; it was first published secretly in the Netherlands in 1909. Tilak is a tempting distractor because he was Savarkar's political contemporary and also gave the revolt a nationalist framing in his writings, but he did not write this specific defining work. Banerjee's memoir 'A Nation in Making' (1925) focuses on the Moderate Congress era, not 1857.
